canberra.title: Something old, something new: Wineries join the Queanbeyan Arts Trail for its 20th anniversary
canberra.snippet: Celebrating 20 years of showcasing the region’s artistic side, the Queanbeyan Arts Trail is finding creative new ways to appreciate art &...
canberra.content:
From ceramics to glass art, plein-air painting to performance, the Arts Trail offers varied opportunities to engage with our region’s art and artists. Photo: Supplied.

Celebrating 20 years of showcasing the region’s artistic side, the Queanbeyan Arts Trail is finding creative new ways to appreciate art – with wineries and motorcycle meet-ups added to the map this year.

The Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council (QPRC) Arts Trail will take place over three weekends in October across Braidwood, Captains Flat, Bungendore and Queanbeyan.

Over 40 venues and activations will participate in an itinerary as broad as the creative disciplines on display.

Finding new ways for tourists and locals alike to experience the region is part of the event’s “all-encompassing” nature, according to Janita Byrne, QPRC Team Leader for Arts and Heritage.

“It’s primarily about promoting our creative industries – because they cover quite a spectrum, from individual practising artists, to groups of artists like the Queanbeyan Art Society, to our incredible state heritage-listed gallery facility, Rusten House Art Centre – and how they draw together artists across the region to not only celebrate their creative output, but to also help generate income for them.

“And the sideline to all of that is that people who come to visit and experience the arts also buy lunches, sometimes stay over and pay for accommodation, and experience other businesses and venues within our region like our historic pubs, or simply walk around and enjoy the ambience of our historic towns.

“The idea is not only to generate tourism visitation, but for our locals to celebrate the amazing things that they do.”

Starting in Braidwood on 3 and 4 October, several local artists will open their home studios to visitors. A collective of around 20 artists will exhibit at the Braidwood Regional Arts Group Gallery with an array of works on paper on sale for under $150.

After securing a beautiful bargain, visitors can take in a music performance at the historic Braidwood District Historical Society Museum ‘Oddfellows’ Hall’ or meet artist-in-residence Jo Parsons over a cheeky gin at Hold Fast Distillery at Trooper’s Rest.

As part of the launch event, artist Ray Monde will showcase his large-scale immersive collaged panels examining queer lived experiences in regional Australia. Photo: Supplied.

Bunker Studio Artists will be one of many artists at their easels for the weekend, sharing their process and inspirations, with artworks available for purchase. Photo: Supplied

The inaugural ‘Sculpture at the Cellar Door’ joins the trail this year, bringing sculpture into the vineyards of the local wineries. Photo: Supplied.

Captains Flat creatives will bookend the trail with unique activations at the start and finish.

On 3 October, Captains Flat Hotel will see the first Blessing of the Bikes event, including a motorcycle “show and shine”, market stalls and food vendors, while on 17 October, the town’s newest retailer, Mama Tierra Collectiva, closes the event with an exhibition from local artisans and food producers.

Bungendore picks up the trail on 10 and 11 October with its broad spectrum of arts and crafts on display.

The Malbon retail collective runs the gamut of artistic expression, from floristry to knitwear and includes the boutique gallery of award-winning photographer Jerusha McDowell.

Around the corner, The Bungendore Bower is a unique creative reuse centre, which keeps creative supplies out of landfill and in the hands of local artists, makers, students and community groups.

If you take your culture with a nice drop, the inaugural Sculpture at the Cellar Door hosted by Lark Hill Winery and Aranya Acres is for you.

“I’m so excited that this year we have managed to get sculptures into the vineyards for our Arts Trail,” said Ms Byrne.

“One of the things that is difficult to exhibit is large outdoor sculptures, because of security issues.

“Pairing them with our local wineries allows us to celebrate those beautiful creative pieces in venues that are keen to have some sort of creative activation as well.

“It is a fabulous pairing for our regional agribusiness and creatives.”

Celebrating its milestone 20th anniversary, the trail will culminate in a citywide “birthday party” on Saturday 17 and Sunday 18 October.

Over 20 galleries, pop-ups, performances and artist studios will open their doors for art appreciation, including a tasting of Lerida Wines at the Queanbeyan Arts Society, the opening of four new exhibitions at Rusten House Art Centre, and a celebration of art and architecture at The Hive.

The Arts Trail will officially launch at The Q Exhibition Space in Queanbeyan on Tuesday, 29 September, at 5:30 pm, with the opening of two new exhibitions in the civic precinct galleries.

To learn more, visit Arts Trail.

canberra.title: Public school teachers stopped work over split and combined classes. How prevalent is the practice?
canberra.snippet: A teacher being asked to cover a class with 90 children. Parents told typical learning arrangements won’t be possible for days due ...
canberra.content:
Split, combined and flexed classes aren’t the same thing – but they are a practice ACT parents don’t want to see used in Canberra’s public schools anymore. Photo: Facebook/AEU ACT.

A teacher being asked to cover a class with 90 children. Parents told typical learning arrangements won’t be possible for days due to staff illness and other leave.

These are two real-life situations that have occurred in Canberra’s public schools as the education sector continues to grapple with workforce shortages and burnout.

Public schools were closed for two hours last Thursday (24 September) as Australian Education Union (AEU) ACT members letterbox-dropped pamphlets across the city about their situation.

It’s the third time work stoppages have occurred this year and another full-day strike is possible for Term Four.

But just how common is the use of split, combined and flexed learning arrangements used across Canberra’s public schools and colleges?

Wait, what’s the difference?

These terms describe different learning arrangements and are not interchangeable.

Split: students from a split class are divided between other suitable classes, but only if there’s capacity in those classrooms under the Class Size Policy. This is generally used in primary schools when there is no in-built or external relief available, and there’s no ability to use school leader teaching hours to cover the class instead.

Combined (sometimes referred to colloquially as collapsed classes): if there are significant staffing absences, then classes may be combined above policy sizes.

Flexed (college-only term): if there’s no casual or internal relief available to cover a teacher absence, the class is cancelled and students receive classwork to complete on their own.

In one email example provided by the AEU ACT, parents and carers were told unexpected staff absences were anticipated to impact the school “for the coming days”.

“To ensure students are supported to learn, we will combine classes and provide students with learning experiences in supervised spaces with known staff members,” the email outlined.

“I hope that we can return to typical learning arrangements by early next week.”

How often is this happening?

The short answer: The Education Directorate doesn’t know.

In an interview with Region, Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said this was a system of the autonomous model that ACT’s public schools had been operating under.

This meant the information was kept by each individual school.

“We have limited visibility on what’s happening with split and collapsed classes,” she said.

“We’re seeing [this issue] anecdotally in particular schools, but it is quite widespread across the system.

“For example, colleges are more likely to flex off a class, but primary children need supervision at all times.”

The Education Directorate has a central register of appropriately qualified and registered casual teachers to support schools to backfill absences.

Schools had their own ways of dealing with staffing absences, but not every solution will fit every school.

Work’s underway to allow the Education Directorate to track the number of split, combined and flexed classes at the ACT’s 93 (soon to be 94) public schools.

What will happen in the meantime?

A longer term solution will take time.

“Our focus for the next few years is to understand the problem and then make sure a solution is in place that will work for our schools,” Ms Stephen-Smith said.

One option not on the table is increasing class sizes.

“The pay and conditions offer of 10 September included an enhanced framework to support sustainable class sizes and class composition,” an ACT Government spokesperson said.

“We’ll keep working with unions and staff to address classroom pressures as negotiations continue in good faith.”

ACT Parents has called on families and community members to add their names to a register calling for a prompt resolution to the enterprise bargaining negotiations.

“Teachers’ working conditions are our students’ learning conditions,” a statement read.

“ACT Parents has been clear about the things that matter most to families: enough teachers and school staff, better management of teacher absences, safe and settled classrooms, and the staffing and support needed for teachers to meet the diverse needs of students.

“Our students need a sustainable resolution that supports teachers and school staff and allows students to get on with learning.”

The advocacy group also wants an end to the use of split, flexed and combined classes.

“Students should not routinely lose access to their normal class and teacher because schools cannot cover teacher absences,” the ACT Parents statement read.

“We want [schooling] reforms to deliver better learning conditions for students, but students cannot wait for long-term reform while their learning is being disrupted now.”

canberra.title: Market eats: what does $20 buy you at Jamison’s Trash and Treasure Market?
canberra.snippet: There is something decidedly old-school and utterly basic about the Trash and Treasure Market Jamison – and I mean that as the high...
canberra.content:
Some things in life don’t need improving, and eating warm, sugary donuts in the sunshine is one of them. Photo: Sophia Brady

There is something decidedly old-school and utterly basic about the Trash and Treasure Market Jamison – and I mean that as the highest compliment.

People are simply selling stuff in a carpark. No elaborate setups or curated tables. Just folks trying to make a few dollars, clear out a shed, or share something they have grown, baked or made.

Good-looking Asian vegetables piled high. Talented home cooks sharing their family recipes. Plants. Honey. I even saw chickens. And my personal favourite, the older blokes selling random treasures that would otherwise end up in landfill. Empty glass jars. Old tools. Mechanical parts. Things whose purpose I can only guess at.

Walking past these stalls reminded me of my grandfather.

Every Sunday, he would front up at the equivalent market at Kingsford in Sydney, until he was too frail to attend. To my young eyes, his table was piled high with what looked like old junk. Cables, crockery, car parts and all manner of mysterious objects. He supplemented his pension by selling things he no longer needed.

A product of wartime Russia, he never threw anything away. If something broke, he fixed it. If he did not need it, he figured someone else might. The same approach applied to food. Nothing was wasted.

Long before the phrase existed, he was living the circular economy.

Walking through the market, I found joy in this old-school atmosphere.

Like my grandfather, many traders still prefer cash. Unfortunately, I didn’t know that before I arrived.

After frantically checking my wallet and rummaging through the car, I managed to scrape together exactly $20.

What does $20 buy you for breakfast at the Trash and Treasure Markets Jamison?

That became my challenge.

Kay’s food stall. Photo: Trash and Treasure Market Jamison Facebook

Kay’s Food

My first stop cost $3.

For that princely sum, I got a piping hot khao porridge wrapped in banana leaf. When I opened it, I found a comforting mix of mung beans and pork.

It was creamy and sweet.

Piping hot khao porridge wrapped in banana leaf. Photo: Sophia Brady

Soft, glutinous and wonderfully wholesome, definitely the type of food that warms you from the inside out.

Kay runs the stall herself, serving Thai home cooking. Takeaway containers filled with goodies, including Thai sausages, pork larb, mango sticky rice, and various forms of jerky, are all available to take away.

Yeden’s Dumplings

My biggest spend of the day was $10 at Yeden’s Dumplings.

The sizeable queue suggested it would be money well spent.

Pork, beef and vegetarian dumplings were available, but there was one catch … no mixing and matching. Commitment was required.

Thankfully, a fellow market-goer standing beside me volunteered her recommendation.

“The vegetarian ones are my favourite.”

Decision made.

Some of the best dumplings in Canberra. Photo: Sophia Brady

Eight generously sized Bhutanese dumplings later, I was very glad I took her advice.

The dough was excellent and the filling featured cheese, raw onion and plenty of fresh flavour. Served with a spicy, house-made chilli sauce, they delivered unexpected complexity.

They were bloody delicious.

In fact, they might be some of the best dumplings in Canberra.

Donut Factory

The lure and smell of fresh, hot cinnamon donuts were strong, so I handed over $5 for six.

Some things in life don’t need improving, and eating warm, sugary donuts in the sunshine is one of them.

Simple. Perfect.

So, I had a three-course meal for $18! Some of the best value money I have spent on food this year! And I still had $2 left in cash, which I dropped into one of the donation buckets positioned at the market entrances.

The Rotary Club of Belconnen has run the market for more than 50 years, raising millions of dollars for community projects in the process, and I hope they continue for 50 more.

Trash and Treasure Market Jamison is on every Sunday from 6:30 am to 12:30 pm in the Jamison Centre carpark in Macquarie.

canberra.title: Single mother ‘overwhelmed’ by thrift shop owner’s generous donation
canberra.snippet: Fyshwick thrift shop The Shed has gifted one lucky Canberran a car as part of a special giveaway to a person in need. The Shed’s ow...
canberra.content:
26 September 2026

Join the conversation

1

Owner of Fyshwick thrift shop The Shed, Adam Charif, said he knew he had made the right decision in his car giveaway as soon as he gave Karen a hug. Photo: The Shed.

Fyshwick thrift shop The Shed has gifted one lucky Canberran a car as part of a special giveaway to a person in need.

The Shed’s owner Adam Charif originally owned the Toyota Camry but, after upgrading to a newer vehicle and rarely using it, he decided to find a local who needed the car more than him.

Mr Charif put out a call online for people to nominate who they believed most needed the car.

He was inundated with more than 100 nominations and he and other staff spent days deciding who was the best fit.

Mr Charif said it was important to find a person he knew would benefit from the car but also someone who would truly value it as well.

“At The Shed, we always like to give back to the community,” he said.

“Every Christmas we do the vouchers … this time, we wanted to do something for our birthday and I thought, what better way to give away a good quality car.

“We had so many applicants and so many people that needed a car. I wish I had more cars to give because it just showed me how much it’s needed in the Canberra community.

“Growing up, my mum didn’t have a car and I learnt how difficult it is to go without. So it was important to me to find someone who needed it, could use it and look after it.”

After the vetting process was done, he and the team at The Shed settled on who they believed most needed a car.

“We gave it to a lovely lady named Karen. When we told her she was the one who was getting the car, her reaction was amazing,” Mr Charif said.

“It was clear to us, as soon as she turned the key in the car, that we had made the right decision. Karen stood out amongst everyone else.

“Her sister was the one to nominate her. She wrote to us about the difficult time that she had gone through and we thought that this was our little way of helping her out.”

Karen was in the store when she got the news. However, she was unaware she had even been nominated.

“I was in the shop, Adam was following me around from the moment I walked in and then he threw me the keys and told me to catch,” she said.

“I knew about the giveaway, but I had no clue I was in the running. I was completely overwhelmed and so extremely grateful that another human being could be so giving.”

Karen said that prior to receiving the car, she had been borrowing one from a friend while trying to save up money for her own.

“It makes such a difference for me. I’ve got two kids. I’m recently a single parent, so for me to actually own a car without having to a save up …” she said.

“I can give my loan car back to my friend and I now have something I can actually own. I can put the insurance on it properly and I can feel a lot more comfortable knowing that it’s mine now.”

Karen said Mr Charif’s generosity has inspired her to give forward whenever she can.

“I honestly don’t know how I can thank someone as generous as Adam,” she said.

“I just know that when he pays it forward, he feels good and now that’s what I’m going to do because I just want everyone to feel the way I did receiving that level of generosity.”

canberra.title: 2024 election pledge for new Molonglo police station blows out to beyond 2027
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s promised Molonglo police station is not expected to reach the approval stage until late 2027, with the ACT Government st...
canberra.content:
Marisa Paterson said planning work is continuing on the Molonglo Police Station. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Canberra’s promised Molonglo police station is not expected to reach the approval stage until late 2027, with the ACT Government still unable to say when construction will begin or the station will open.

Police, Fire and Emergency Services Minister Marisa Paterson revealed the new timeline during a Legislative Assembly debate, saying planning work was continuing and a report on planning considerations was expected later this year.

“The Molonglo Police Station is expected to progress to the approval stage in late 2027,” she said.

Dr Paterson said the subsequent statutory approval process was expected to take about 12 to 18 months, with a detailed delivery timeline to be confirmed as those approvals progressed.

Labor committed ahead of the 2024 ACT election to include a new police station in the Molonglo Town Centre. Government implementation documents subsequently listed the anticipated delivery timeframe as “more than 12 months.”

The new timeline came as Canberra Liberals MLAs Ed Cocks and Deborah Morris moved a motion calling for a stronger visible police presence in Molonglo and certainty over when the promised station would be built.

Ms Morris pointed to residents’ accounts of attempted break-ins, people checking cars and gates at night and neighbours setting up WhatsApp groups to alert each other to suspicious activity.

She argued residents had expected Labor’s election commitment to result in a station being delivered, rather than an extended planning process.

“The government should be able to tell this community when construction of the police station will begin and when the doors will open,” she said.

Dr Paterson acknowledged reported offences across Molonglo had increased by about 12 per cent, from 594 in 2024-25 to 665 in 2025-26, but said the increase needed to be viewed alongside rapid population and residential growth.

However, she added that burglaries fell by about 32 per cent, stolen motor vehicles by 13 per cent, theft offences by about five per cent over the same period and property offences by 50 per cent. Offences against the person increased from 86 to 109, while traffic offences rose from 108 to 176.

Dr Paterson said ACT Policing used an intelligence-led deployment model, with officers sent according to crime trends, emerging risks and calls for service rather than simply the location of police stations.

She said patrols could be adjusted when hotspots emerged and committed to attending another community forum with the Chief Police Officer before the end of the year.

The Greens backed the need for a station but also questioned how long residents were being asked to wait.

“It is a bit disingenuous to promise at the 2024 election that Labor will build a new police station … but what’s not said that it will be built in some distant future date,” the Greens MLA Rebecca Vassarotti told the Assembly.

They said residents’ concerns about break-ins and attempted break-ins were genuine, while arguing police resources should continue to be allocated across Canberra according to evidence and need.

The Greens supported government amendments requiring Dr Paterson to report back to the Assembly in the first sitting period next year, saying they expected the government to provide a clearer delivery timetable then.

Independent MLA Fiona Carrick then successfully amended the motion further, putting another deadline around the project.

Her amendment called on the government to finalise the land subdivision in the Molonglo Town Centre for the police station and either release the block to market or issue a construction tender by the end of 2027.

“There is some funding for planning in the budget, but we still do not have a clear construction timetable and opening date,” Ms Carrick said.

“The police station should not become another example of infrastructure being left to catch up with population growth,” she said.

Her amendment also called for the government to work with ACT Policing to ensure an appropriate visible police presence and patrols in Molonglo and nearby areas while the station is being planned.

The Liberals backed Ms Carrick’s changes, with Mr Cocks saying they restored some of the elements relating to visible policing that had been altered by the government’s amendments.

The amended motion ultimately passed the Assembly.

australia.title: Free the Strip! Melburnians fight back against outlawing of much-loved picnic spot
australia.snippet: A council ban on drinking on the median strip in Canning Street, Carlton, sparks a peaceful protest featuring punch bowls, chips and laug...
australia.content:
It looked like a typical spring evening on Melbourne’s Canning Street when a few dozen picnickers gathered on the grassy median strip on Friday, with drinks in hand.

People in one group who’d come with a full alfresco setting chattered as they ladled punch out of a glass bowl on a wooden table, set with a tablecloth and yellow flowers in a vase. Others sat on picnic blankets, passing around bags of chips.

What set this gathering apart was that it was actually against the rules, given the new ban against drinking on the strip. And the picnic had been organised in protest, part of a political saga that is unfolding on one of inner Melbourne’s most beloved streets.

It began on Monday, when a local bar and bottle shop, the Wine Corner Store, announced on Instagram that, “due to a few unrelenting miserable neighbours who have been non-stop complaining to the council”, consuming alcohol had been outlawed on the median strips on Drummond, Rathdowne and Canning streets in Carlton North.

The council was reverting to a former classification of the median strips – which are much wider than a typical nature strip – with the effect that they are no longer treated as park spaces. The council said residents had complained about noise, rubbish and unsafe behaviour.

The community fought back to keep a tradition that has endured for many years. While the council ban followed an initial 29-signature petition that a resident submitted in August, a counter petition calling on council to revoke the ban gathered more than 7,707 signatures in just a few days.

The protest drinks on Friday were civilised.

Amid the uproar – and with people loosely uniting under a banner of Free the Strip! – Adam Pulford, the Greens candidate for the seat of Brunswick at the state election, had posted an invitation on social media for people to join him for a peaceful protest.

People milled around, chatting and offering each other drinks and nibbles, talking about the importance of preserving places for building connections outside work and home.

“We need to be building community spaces and not getting rid of them,” said Sam Drummond, who attended the gathering. “Particularly post-Covid, there are very few spaces where people can come together and meet in public, in person.”

Others on the strip on Friday had heeded a call from a Canning Street resident, Rachel Richmond, to gather for the same purpose. As the groups coalesced, Richmond said it was “the most civilised act of civil disobedience I’ve ever participated in”.

“This might seem like a very ridiculously middle class thing to protest,” she said. “I mean, it’s literal champagne socialism but honestly, sitting underneath it is an issue about public space and public enjoyment of space.”

The only disorderly incident the Guardian witnessed on the median strip on Friday was a minor skirmish between a chihuahua and a labrador, both on leads.

However, local councillor Edward Crossland, who represents the Carlton North ward, said there had been “genuine amenity concerns”, especially from people living around the Wine Corner Store, and he believed it was unfair the council had been portrayed in a negative way.

Nevertheless, Crossland said council staff had gone too far in banning drinking outright. “There are some people that have been behaving not fantastically but the majority of people are just having a picnic,” he said.

Crossland said he was working with the council staff to prepare a motion for their next meeting in October, which he anticipated would re-classify the median as open space, and look at “particular” measures to address concerns surrounding the Wine Corner Store.

The venue’s owner, Steve Misfud-Ellul, said his business had wrongly copped the blame for large groups choosing to stop on the grass near the wine bar.

“We simply sell retail drinks to people and they choose to stop where they stop,” he said. “Ninety-nine per cent of the time it’s people sitting, picnicking on a patch of grass, with the loudest noise being laughing.”

Misfud-Ellul also stressed the council was not to blame.

“The council actually were fantastic and they acted on every complaint; they came through, they check and they saw there was no problem,” he said.

The premier, Ben Carroll, waded in on Friday, sharing a post on social media that said: “Consider this unbanned. Because if council doesn’t reverse it, we will reverse it for them.”

On Saturday, the Yarra mayor, Stephen Jolly, said he was working with Misfud-Ellul, locals and the council to sort out the issue, but reverting to the status quo wasn’t an option.

“My solution is either to get an outdoor trading permit for the bar as per what many bars on Brunswick and Smith Streets have; or work with the state government to reclassify the median strip to allow (better managed) drinking and chilling on the strip,” he wrote on Instagram.

“It’s slightly more complicated than it seems, but nevertheless it’s fixable.”

Australian Associated Press contributed to this report

australia.title: Cooler roofs will prevail: colours and coatings to help beat the heat
australia.snippet: Even before adding solar panels, your roof can help you keep cool and lower your energy bills Change by degrees offers life hacks and sus...
australia.content:
With an historic El Niño under way in the Pacific, Australia could face record temperatures this summer. For those in hot homes, reflective roof coatings can be a cost-effective way to beat the heat.

The upstairs bedrooms and office in Nic Jacobson’s two storey home in inner-suburban Adelaide used to get unbearably hot, even when his large air-conditioning system was running flat out.

“The insulation was not great, so I did some work upgrading that,” says Jacobson, an engineer who has worked in renewable energy for two decades. But after his changes, Jacobson could still feel intense heat radiating through the flat metal roof and blue board and plaster stud walls.

“The western wall in particular copped a lot of sun; because it was the second storey there was no shading from trees or adjacent buildings,” he says.

After Jacobson painted the roof and wall with a heat-reflective coating, the change was immediate.

“It definitely lowered the heat penetrating the house upstairs,” he says. Although he can’t quantify the savings, he reckons he cut his air conditioning bill significantly. “I’m very happy with the decision I made,” he says. “I think it’s a good product and look for opportunities to recommend it.”

Most Australian house roofs are either metal or tiled, though many apartments have concrete roofs. The majority are medium to dark in colour, according to CSIRO’s Australian Housing Data, even though lighter shades generally reflect more heat.

Light colours and reflective surfaces

Shane Strudwick says Australia has a massive blind spot when it comes to the role roof surfaces and dark colours play in heating homes. Strudwick distributes Super Therm, the coating Jacobson applied to his home, which is more commonly used on commercial and industrial properties.

A water-based ceramic paint developed by Nasa for the space shuttle, Super Therm repels infrared radiation, preventing roofs from heating up and transferring heat inside the house.

In a basic trial on a 22C day in Adelaide, Strudwick coated some concrete roof tiles and left others untreated. By 1pm, he says, the surface temperature of the original tiles had hit 60C, while those with a single coat of Super Therm were just 26C.

He says the cost of coating a roof will generally pay for itself in lower energy bills in three to five years, though he cautions that payback times vary depending on the original surface and previous household energy use.

A cost-benefit analysis by researchers at the University of New South Wales concluded that the cost of coating an otherwise functional roof is recovered not just through energy savings, but also by prolonging the life of the roof itself (which also reduces waste going to landfill).

Leading cool roof researcher Prof Sebastian Pfautsch says people who’ve unwittingly bought homes with dark roofs find themselves “in a real schemozzle” when summer hits, especially if their roof is covered in cement tiles rather than metal.

“Cement has a much greater thermal mass, so it takes much longer to cool down,” explains Pfautsch, who is based at Western Sydney University.

Pfautsch says retrofitting a roof with a reflective coating should be a first step, ahead of other options such as installing solar panels or better insulation.

Solar panels can help cool a roof by converting radiant energy into electricity. Yet photovoltaic systems become less efficient if they get too hot, so installing panels on a dark, heat-absorbent roof is a false economy.

“The first and most cost-effective thing to do is coat it,” says Pfautsch. “After that, put solar on. Once you have a light-coloured roof your solar panels work more effectively.”

Sky gardens and cool coatings

Combining panels with plants can create the triple win of a “bio-solar” roof – saving energy through insulation, boosting solar power output and increasing biodiversity.

But planting a garden on top of your home can be challenging and expensive. In most cases, recoating a roof is cheaper and simpler.

“There are many ways to retrofit a house to keep it cool and save energy but applying a coat of paint on the roof is one of the most efficient and low cost”, says Prof Chiara Neto, a physical chemist at the University of Sydney.

“It could save up to 40% of your energy bill, especially if you have an older building with poor insulation and a dark roof.”

Neto developed a film that reflects 96% of heat from the sun and also collects water.

In 2022, Neto and her former PhD student founded a startup called Dewpoint to commercialise their invention. It hopes to retail the coating in Australia at a price competitive with existing premium paints. The product is undergoing trials in the Middle East, Asia and Australia. “People want to see it in action in a real building and measure energy efficiency over time,” Neto says.

“The paint is designed to let go of droplets so they roll off the roof readily and can be easily collected before they evaporate,” she explains. And because the roof stays cooler for longer, it’s more efficient at condensing moisture from the atmosphere. Plus, it’s self-cleaning, which maintains its reflective properties.

Pfautsch says Super Therm is one product already on the market that is worth considering.

“I have no shares and I’m not a sales agent for them,” he stresses. But some products don’t deliver what they promise, he warns, noting that Dulux paid a $400,000 penalty in 2016 for making unfounded claims about the temperature-reducing properties of two paints.

A heat-reflecting roof will generally be light-coloured but doesn’t have to be white, Pfautsch says, so it’s possible to avoid an excessively bright roof that reflects glare into nearby buildings. Neto notes that heat-reflective roof coatings mostly have a positive impact on nearby residents.

“If all roofs were treated, that could reduce the air temperature in a suburb by two or three degrees,” she says. “By preventing surfaces from getting hot, removing heat and passively cooling the surface, neighbouring buildings will benefit.”

If you’re suffering under a hot roof, Pfautsch encourages you to do yourself, your neighbours and the planet a favour.

“It’s an ethical question of how you want to live in your community and make your contribution,” he says.

australia.title: OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemma
australia.snippet: As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI race When the Austral...
australia.content:
When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent.

He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.”

But Albanese noted, too, that two countries – the US and China – would dominate the world’s response to the new technology.

“The truth is they’re the big two giants here, and so we want to see cooperation,” Albanese said.

“The US is essentially ahead of China when it comes to the race that is on for the development of this new technology. But it is in the world’s interests that there be engagement.”

Days later, Albanese used the global attention of the United Nations general assembly meeting in New York to reveal that Australia’s government healthcare system, Medicare, had been attacked by an OpenAI agent in June, but that it was three months before his government was told.

Again he warned of “the potential risks of allowing frontier AI to develop too fast without guardrails”.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, skipped the general assembly in favour of a bilateral meeting with the US president, where he emphasised the responsibility to manage AI “for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people”.

But the president of the United States – the nation which is the global leader in artificial intelligence – used his general assembly address to insist he would only encourage, not restrain, the AI race.

Alarms sounding

To little fanfare earlier in the week, the UN’s independent international scientific panel on AI warned a threshold had already been crossed.

There was, the panel, said: “no assurance that humans can reliably keep AI agents under control today, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity”.

The Australian government had known the reality of this for more than a week. OpenAI had known it more than a month.

Two days after the panel’s statement, the Australian prime minister belatedly revealed an OpenAI agent had hacked medical data held by Australia’s universal health care provider, Medicare.

No patient data had been accessed, but the agent had gained unauthorised access to “non-public files”.

OpenAI’s agent hacked the government sites in June of this year. OpenAI discovered its agent had gone rogue in August. It did not tell the Australian government until 10 September, and then only with a solitary email to a generic public email address not checked until the next day. The prime minister was informed on 18 September.

It was another week before the Australian people were told.

Australia has promised, if it is possible, to lay criminal charges, though this is complicated by the fact that OpenAI claims the hack was committed by an AI agent – apparently acting beyond its instructions (euphemised by OpenAI as “misaligned behaviour”) – not a person.

The hack on Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service portal, as well as three other government sites, follows the Hugging Face incident in July, in which autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI broke out of their isolated testing environments, coordinated themselves into a “swarm” and launched a cyber-attack on competitor AI platform Hugging Face.

The UN panel, investigating that attack, warned “the traditional method of safeguarding is unravelling” as AI agents act autonomously to breach protections.

“The default interpretation and immediate lesson is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, and safeguards are not advancing at the pace of capabilities. The more insidious and grave concern is that current training methods can lead agents to adopt goals of their own, knowingly violate safety instructions, and conceal their actions.”

Twenty countries (including Australia) and the EU this week signed a statement arguing the rapid development of frontier AI models posed serious risks to safety and security if not properly managed.

“AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law.”

Too soon?

Even those running AI companies have warned the technology is developing too rapidly for humans to control.

Appearing before the UN security council this week, OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, warned: “some of the things people working to build AI have said are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies”.

“As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.”

But there are at least two – very loud – voices in opposition to any external regulation of the AI industry.

Elon Musk, who co-founded OpenAI with Altman before falling out with him, said in a recent interview the “smart move” would be to have the “leading AI companies at least just meet or have some sort of call once every few weeks and just discuss any safety and security issues”.

Musk said AI would probably be beyond the control of humans within a decade, and that humanity should “enjoy the ride”.

“I still think there’s risk associated with AI and robots. It’s not zero … my sort of philosophical conclusion is to look on the bright side. I can’t see any way to really stop this incredible momentum of AI and robots.

“If there was a stop button, we probably shouldn’t press it, because the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all.”

Donald Trump used his speech to the UN general assembly to attempt to rebrand AI, and insist it should never be reined in.

“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now,” the US president said.

Trump wants to re-label artificial intelligence “superintelligence”.

“I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.

“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.”

Trump said the US was “leading China by a lot” in AI, and would continue to do so “safely and responsibly”.

“Whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”

australia.title: ‘Robust little’ vessel begins treacherous 22,000km journey around Antarctica in the name of climate science
australia.snippet: Powered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissio...
australia.content:
A small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap around Antarctica and may not return for months.

The seven-metre craft, which looks like a large kayak in hi-vis orange, is expected to travel about 22,000km through inhospitable waters, propelled by powerful westerly winds and energy from the sun. The journey is seven times the distance between Sydney and Perth.

Along the way, it is expected to encounter massive waves, freezing temperatures, ferocious winds, and even the odd curious seal or albatross.

The mission? To collect data on carbon dioxide in the ocean and atmosphere, to help scientists better understand the role of ocean sinks.

Dr Elizabeth Shadwick, a principal research scientist at the CSIRO, said that after leaving Hobart the vessel would travel east towards New Zealand, “eventually scooching through the Drake Passage between the bottom of South America and Antarctica, then coming along past South Africa and back to us here, where we’ll pick it up.”

She hoped to see it again in seven to nine months.

The autonomous vehicle made by the US maritime company Saildrone was designed to withstand the intrepid voyage, with a heavy keel keeping it upright, a rudder to steer and a fixed solar sail poking above the surface. It would be remotely monitored by the company, who would check in regularly via satellite, and, if necessary, nudge it in the right direction.

“It’s already been bashed around pretty heavily,” Shadwick said. “It’s quite a robust little device. We saw some eight metres of waves just the day after we deployed it and a 35-knot wind.”

Measurements taken throughout its journey – including wind speed, atmospheric pressure, solar radiation, ocean temperature, salinity and chlorophyll, as well as carbon dioxide levels in the water and air – were expected to assist scientists in better understanding the role that oceans play in global heating.

“The ocean is doing all of us a great service by absorbing about a third of anthropogenic or human emissions every year,” Shadwick said, and the Southern Ocean, around Antarctica, played a significant role. “If we want to continue to rely on this ocean service of absorbing our human emissions, we need to understand how it might change in the future.”

Crewed research vessels that travelled between Hobart and Antarctica traversed only a limited patch of the ocean, she said. The autonomous craft would gather data over a greater distance and time, including crucial measurements during the polar winter.

The vessel is the first in a fleet of four. Others are planned to be launched at three-monthly intervals. They will be spread across the Southern, Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans, particularly during winter.

The scientists will be able to access information in near real time via a mission portal, and once the vessels return to home base, all data and observations will undergo quality checks before they are made available for further research.

Dr Pep Canadell, a chief research scientist at the CSIRO, said for every tonne of carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels, about 500kg were removed by ocean and forest sinks. “This is like a 50% discount on climate change,” he said.

But the amount absorbed by the oceans could change due to multiple drivers: warming waters, westerly winds, melting ice, ocean acidification and the hole in the ozone layer. Observations would enable scientists to more accurately model these processes and understand how they could change in the future, he said.

The University of New South Wales professor Matthew England, who studies the role of ocean circulation in global climate but was not involved in the research project, said measuring how much the oceans absorbed and how that was changing was critical.

“We’ve obviously got a surge of emissions going into our atmosphere. Both the terrestrial vegetation on land and the oceans absorb a big chunk of that,” he said. “We need to track that carbon uptake and understand exactly how big the absorption is. If it starts to decline in a significant way, then it tells us that we have an even bigger problem of carbon emission reductions.”

The Southern Ocean was “inhospitable” with huge swells, gale force winds, sea ice and storms. “These are very tough measuring conditions for a research vessel.” So gathering data using an autonomous vehicle, without burning fuel, was “an incredible deployment of technology”, he said.

australia.title: Bruce Pascoe’s new book may spark another culture war. He hopes for ‘decency and intellectual curiosity’ this time
australia.snippet: The Dark Emu author rails against Christianity, capitalism and colonialism – and Shakespeare and Charles Dickens cop a serve too. He’s re...
australia.content:
On the eve of publication of his new book, Bruce Pascoe is steeling himself for potential controversy that could rival the bitter storm that battered and bruised him for years over the 2014 book that rewrote Australian history: Dark Emu.

Where Dark Emu contentiously sought to reframe pre-invasion Australian First Nations people from hunter-gatherers into more complex farmer-cultivators, Pascoe’s new book, The European Mind: Colonialism, Capitalism, Christianity and How to Recover, sheets home the blame for the most heinous excesses of racism and dispossession on to a troika of western shibboleths: Christianity, capitalism and colonialism.

On a hot early spring morning in Sydney, Pascoe – a southern Victorian farmer and celebrated literary author of Yuin, Bunurong and Tasmanian ancestry – sits on a stage at the New South Wales State Library to promote his new book. While “beautiful”, he says the original Mitchell reading room where the event is being hosted is ironically “one of the most colonial” in Sydney, with its early 1900s club atmosphere.

In conversation with Bigambul and Wakka Wakka writer and academic Melanie Saward, he says, with good humour: “I’ll have the noise and these attacks going on [again]. But you know I’m loved by my family, and I’m loved by my Country … Once again there’ll be a storm, you know. I’ll be accused by some of eating kittens. And eating them slowly, which is worse.”

He laughs. But a reticence clearly underscores the nonchalance. For it did get pretty nasty last time, including with renewed allegations questioning the veracity of his Aboriginal identity, and a major academic takedown of his research and methodology.

With his farm-labour wiriness, trademark wild mane of silver hair and long beard, the fit-looking 79-year-old says there have “been times, I admit, when I struggle”.

When we sit in the sunshine after the event to talk about the new book and Australian rules football (he is a diehard Richmond supporter who watched the Fremantle v Swans preliminary final the night before), he sounds tentatively prepared for another pile-on.

Is he ready? “I hope I am. I have been readying myself for it. I think I am about as ready as I can be for it. But look, it’s very difficult to hurt an old man, because you’ve become very aware of how many years you’ve got left – active years I mean. And you can’t bribe an old man because he doesn’t want anything. And you can’t intimidate an old man because he’s going to die anyway soon, so you can’t hurt him. I’m trying to placate myself I think, but I’m also trying to ready myself. I find hatred to be unproductive.

“Realistically you can’t go and write [critically] about capitalism, Christianity and colonialism in a single book and expect not to get a significant reaction … because it deliberately evokes comment and disagreement. These things are very important to people, so I have to be ready for those arguments. But I just hope that, you know, there’s a bit of decency about it and a bit of intellectual curiosity.”

Pascoe’s argument (drawn from a First Nations perspective) is that western religion’s view of “other” spiritual beliefs as inferior, Europe’s innate sense of moral and racial superiority, and capitalism’s insatiable appetite for natural resources drove global First Nations dispossession as equally as a yearning for exploration and mercantile expansion.

First Nations writers, artists and activists the world over have long railed against the insidious effect of capitalism, colonialism and the church on Indigenous people’s generational outcomes. And while Pascoe’s most vociferous critics in the academy and media (chief among whom he cites Australian News Corp outlets) will doubtless comb through every line, the European Mind is anything but a polemic rant. As with Dark Emu, he quotes exhaustively from various western and European colonial and later historical sources. The book includes a four-page bibliography and 14 pages of endnotes.

But it’s hard to deny the marketability of controversy: the literary frisson attached to the elegantly written contentions of such an enigmatic and celebrated writer as Pascoe. With 406,000 copies sold (and 110,000 of the children’s edition), Dark Emu remains one of this country’s highest-selling books in the broad category of Australian history. While a literary storm can be punishing and at times very cruel, the dividends can also be significant.

And so some of the past’s most prominent possessors of European mindsets are hauled to Pascoe’s historical guillotine. Among them are Baden Powell (celebrated British army officer and founder of the Boy Scouts), “dismayed when his foe surrenders” rather than give him the desired valiant scrap on the battlefield; Lord Wolseley (one of the foremost British army generals at the vanguard of late 19th century imperial expansion), revelling in “rapture-giving delight which attack upon an enemy affords”; Winston Churchill (“a horrible bastard”, the author contends, at his library event) relishing his battlefield experiences. Even Walt Whitman, The Bard and Charles Dickens cop a serve.

Pascoe writes in the European Mind: “The American poet, Walt Whitman, was a fervent supporter of the white establishment; Charles Dickens rooted for the Empire in India; and Shakespeare, while sublimely sardonic, seemed resigned to the fact that the world would be a treacherous place dominated by big men.”

He contends that European colonial expansion drew its moral weight and certainty from many institutional and cultural sources, but not least through the Catholic church and Pope Alexander V1’s 1493 papal bull, The Doctrine of Discovery. It deemed that exploring Christians could rightfully claim territory where Indigenes did not know the name Jesus Christ.

There is a personal warmth about Pascoe which drives his yearning to “yarn” about his writing – to discuss his ideas and contentions with those who will take exception. He seems surprised that so many of his most vociferous critics wouldn’t engage him on civil grounds last time.

In this latter part of his life he wants a discussion – national, universal and personal – that might lead to better human understanding among different faiths and traditional knowledge holders.

“I do feel an obligation to be hopeful because I’ve got grandchildren. But I also have to interrogate myself about this, because I don’t want to be talking bullshit just because it sounds good. I have to ask myself, ‘Do you really believe this?’ And I do. I think there is enough goodness in the world. The vast majority of us want decency, we want love, we want care. We want to look after each other and the world. And we’ve been diverted by a very small, powerful group – people who hate everything,” he says.

“We need to talk – to find common ground.”

He speaks, as he writes in the book, passionately and lovingly about his deeply Christian mother and his discussions with her about his terminal disenchantment with the church when he was young. While coming from diametrically opposite positions, their respectful conversations, he says, inspired far greater mutual understanding about many aspects of life.

He offers this relationship as a template, perhaps, for broader discussions about belonging, spiritual belief, faith and personal identity.

“I was sceptical [of Christian religion] from a very early age … but I understand people’s spiritual needs because I have that as well.”

He believes most people of religion – regardless of faith – are pursuing the same thing: peace and togetherness.

“I don’t believe that most Christians want to see Pete Hegseth praying for violence [for “overwhelming violence of action against those who deserve no mercy”, as the United States Secretary for War put it] and I still can’t believe how [Christian] clerics let that go unchallenged.”

This discussion of “belief” leads us back to his beloved AFL – to the “joy” and “beauty” of the previous night’s final.

Some will always regard the game as an exemplar of Indigenous cultural fusion with the Australian colonial. Some historians, meanwhile, will always hotly contest this.

“The game’s spirit is Aboriginal,” Pascoe says.

Discuss. With civility.

  • The European Mind: Colonialism, Capitalism, Christianity and How to Recover is out 28 September through Magabala books

world.title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
world.snippet: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government There are growing fears of a retu...
world.content:
There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.

About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.

On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.

The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.

Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.

A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”

The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.

The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.

In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.

Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”

The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.

Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.

The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.

It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.

On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.

In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions.

AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years
world.snippet: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market Nils Pratley: Does this mark the end of London’s ...
world.content:
A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.

Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.

The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.

Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.

Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.

“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.

“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”

Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”

Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.

Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.

Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.

Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.

The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.

Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

world.title: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl
world.snippet: Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality One of South Africa...
world.content:
One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls.

Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child.

Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk.

South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year.

Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.”

Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet.

The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him.

Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24.

Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct.

“Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.”

When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation.

Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift.

Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.

world.title: Healthcare in Africa ‘under growing strain’ after US withdrawal from aid programs, report warns
world.snippet: Accra Reset’s report states countries in the region and global south should take greater control of their health development after USAID ...
world.content:
The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put healthcare in Africa and the global south “under growing strain” a new report warns.

The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.

The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.

A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.

The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.

External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.

The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.

Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.

At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m after the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.

The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.

“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”

Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.

“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”

The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. About 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of more than 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.

The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.

The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.

world.title: Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation deals
world.snippet: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is o...
world.content:
Nika’s story

No one would tell the shackled detainees onboard the US immigration plane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out.

Their destination was Central African Republic (CAR), a country few of them had even heard of.

Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane.

Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there.

After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east.

“They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything about Africa.”

The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her?

Nika is one of more than 25,000 people deported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk.

Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.

In order to compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.

It has tracked more than 100 flights that have carried migrants and asylum seekers to 28 different countries. This is likely to be an undercount as the consortium’s dataset only includes flights it was able to independently verify.

The pace of flights is increasing. After an initial wave during the opening months of the second Trump administration, the number of deportations spiked in August again when, according to a count by Human Rights First, a record 16 flights carried people to 13 different countries that were not their own.

A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that third-country removals were unlawful, arguing that they violated due process because people are not notified with enough time to mount a legal challenge to the decision to send them to another country. Human rights lawyers suggested this should immediately ground third-country deportation flights. The government is expected to appeal against the judgment, and to press ahead with its policy.

A state department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority” and “we are unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”. They added: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”

The Trump administration has said the people it deports are criminals. Yet documents obtained by the Washington Post as part of this project show that a majority of the 35 countries that have signed deals with the US have said they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.


The people forced on to planes include those who spent most of their lives in the US, parents detained on the school run, the adult children of elderly relatives who depend on them for care.

Many are people whose fear of returning home was deemed so credible that immigration judges barred their removal from the US. Nika had been granted “withholding of removal”, a protection for individuals who may face severe harm in their country of origin but are ineligible for asylum. On 28 May, not only was she released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s custody, but she was eligible to find a job, to work, and to stay.

The rug pull

Nika’s lawyer, Sahar Jalili, is Iranian and, like her client, studied in Tehran. She took the case when she was pregnant, and often worked past the point of exhaustion. “That could be me,” she said of Nika.

Combing through the case file, Jalili was shocked to learn ICE had officially decided to send Nika to CAR’s capital, Bangui, just eight days before a judge ordered her release from the detention centre. Her uncle’s family had prepared a room for her in Los Angeles. It took her two days to get there, and she spent a week with them, unfurling, after 18 months of hell.

Her re-arrest on 8 June, during what ICE officers had presented as a routine check-in, felt like cruelty for cruelty’s sake, Jalili said.

Nika said she had finished her appointment and left when an officer called her uncle and asked him to drive her back to pick up some papers.

This time there were new questions. A man took Nika’s fingerprints, then her photograph, Jalili said. “Then he came back accompanied by a female ICE officer, and they said put your hands above your head.” She said she was arrested, handcuffed and led to the basement.

Nika felt numb, she said, as she was transferred out of the detention facility that evening. Anti-ICE demonstrators smacked their palms on the side of the van as she passed through protests that had become a regular feature in LA.

For Jalili, the previous two days had already been a blur, as she and her colleagues battled to save two other Iranian women from being put on the same plane for Bangui. The lawyers managed to get the other two women off the plane, but not Nika. The only difference between them was that Nika was detained last, so by the time a network of immigration lawyers had learned of her case, there was not enough time before the flight departed.

Jalili said she begged every ICE officer: “Give me two days. Just two days.” She recalled: “They told me that they had respected the judge’s order to release her. But they’d never promised not to send her to a third country.”
